conflicts.point: Whether mandatory structural separation of AI layers destroys necessary hardware-software co-design or enables modular standard interfaces.

positions.stance: Argues that separating silicon, cloud, and models introduces prohibitive latency and communication overhead that breaks distributed training loops and stalls performance scaling.
Argues that modular standards like tensor-parallel communication layers can separate physical hardware from model architecture without sacrificing performance.

conflicts.point: Whether independent audit boards and structural separation are necessary to prevent catastrophic safety risks or constitute bureaucratic delays that harm public health innovation.

positions.stance: Prioritizes speed of capability scaling to accelerate medical discoveries and maintain geopolitical advantage over authoritarian competitors.
Prioritizes pre-deployment institutional oversight and operational firewalls to prevent runaway systemic risks from uncontained AI systems.

verdicts.conflict: Whether mandatory structural separation of AI layers destroys necessary hardware-software co-design or enables modular standard interfaces.
verdicts.rationale: Both positions rely on projected engineering outcomes without concrete data from large-scale unbundling attempts. The accelerationist position identifies real latency risks in distributed training, but the safetyist position correctly points to historical precedents like FCC telecommunications unbundling. The debate remains deadlocked because neither side provides verifiable timelines or measurable performance thresholds for separation.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Controlled empirical benchmarks comparing the training throughput of tightly integrated proprietary clusters against modular stacks using standardized interconnects.

verdicts.conflict: Whether independent audit boards and structural separation are necessary to prevent catastrophic safety risks or constitute bureaucratic delays that harm public health innovation.
verdicts.rationale: This conflict balances unquantified systemic tail risks against immediate geopolitical and medical research benefits. Safety proponents emphasize catastrophic failure modes, whereas accelerationists point to measurable current gains in healthcare and competitive advantage. The criteria lack a shared metric to weigh speculative long-term safety against concrete present-day applications.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Quantitative risk assessments establishing the precise probability and severity of uncontained model failures relative to the opportunity cost of delayed deployments.
